A non-invertible symmetry can be viewed as a symmetry with local degrees of freedom, where the action of one instance may require multiple realizations to be implemented. This concept applies generally, regardless of whether the system in question is classical or quantum, invertible or non-invertible. We explore the non-invertible anomaly in both the context of classical mechanics and quantum field theories, using examples for illustration. Specifically, in classical mechanics, we demonstrate how an non-invertible symmetry gives rise to a non-commutative symmetry and an anomaly. In the case of quantum field theories, we identify an non-invertible anomaly as a difference between two possible actions of symmetry on local observables. Both cases are exemplified through the study of systems possessing a non-invertible symmetry under the action of $G_2$, a group with a complex representation. Our research highlights the significance of non-invertible symmetry in the phenomenon of phase transitions with an Adler-Bell-Jackiw anomaly. The analysis reveals that read-write systems can tolerate specific levels of background synchronization error without compromising data integrity, providing a framework for future error-tolerant background synchronization designs. This analysis is grounded in real-world distributed storage systems, such as Google's File System and Amazon S3. Additionally, the paper explores the challenges of detecting background synchronization errors and proposes a novel method to verify background synchronization in systems that use append-based log structures. A proof-of-concept prototype, implemented for HDFS, demonstrates the feasibility of detecting such errors. researchers have investigated the behavior of water near a simulated cell membrane composed of fatty acid molecules. The study found that water molecules are drawn into a more ordered state when surrounded by the fatty acid chains, but also that this ordering changes significantly when the water is closer to the center of the micelle rather than the outer surface. Ultimately, the study provides a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between water and fatty acid molecules, paving the way for further research in this area. However, existing social engineering attacks centered on microblogs primarily aim to deceive users into downloading malicious software or revealing sensitive information. Our research diverges from this focus, targeting users' purchasing decisions through specific products rather than universal information. To achieve this goal, an attacker must first establish a credible identity as a seasoned buyer, then utilize various persuasive strategies to deceive potential sellers. To study these tactics, we created a platform for online haggling and recruited 40 skilled attackers to engage in transactions. Through live experiments, we discovered that successful attackers employ several key techniques: establishing a credible identity, initiating conversations with a limited number of sellers, and negotiating with a single seller after gaining trust. Our findings highlight the need for social media platforms to develop more effective measures to prevent haggling scams, particularly those targeting users' purchasing decisions. Our research also provides valuable insights for social engineers seeking to hone their haggling skills. To facilitate further research, we are sharing our platform, data, and attack strategies with the research community. Research has led to the development of several methods to address this challenge, including active learning techniques that aim to optimize dataset collection by prioritizing samples that will significantly improve model accuracy when labeled. While existing active learning methods primarily focus on enhancing model performance, our proposed approach, semi-supervised active learning, also prioritizes maintaining model robustness by preventing it from overfitting to noisy, unlabeled data. We introduce a new method to assess robustness based on the model's margin, which measures the average distance between predicted classes. This average distance is calculated using the mean absolute difference between predicted probabilities across multiple models with varying levels of noise. We developed a noise injection technique to simulate diverse training conditions and proposed a simple yet effective ensemble method to calculate the margin. We tested our approach on several datasets and compared it to established active learning methods, including query-by-committee and entropy-based techniques. The results show that our semi-supervised active learning method outperforms these methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness. We also explored the impact of different data augmentation methods and the effect of varying label availability on our approach. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexandrevandeneede/SSAL. Our pre-trained models can be found on Pytorch Hub at https://pytorch-hub.com/vandeneede/ssal. A relevant problem emerged - finding the optimal superimposed signal to maximize the probability of correct symbol detection. While current research has made significant progress in creating models with strong generalization capabilities for specific tasks, there is a lack of models with similar capabilities for graph representation learning. In response to this, we introduce the Generalization Graph Generator (GGG), a cutting-edge approach for creating highly generalizable graph neural networks (GNNs) through the use of a trainable graph generation system. By enabling the flexible creation of graphs with varying node features, edge structures, and labels, GGG significantly expands the scope of possible training datasets. In line with this goal, we propose the Node-Averaged Graph Generator (NAGG) model, which demonstrates exceptional generalization performance by effectively averaging node features during the graph generation process. Through rigorous testing across multiple benchmark datasets, we verify that both GGG and NAGG outperform existing state-of-the-art models in both semi-supervised and unsupervised graph classification tasks. In addition, we conduct comprehensive ablation studies to illustrate the pivotal role of both trainable graph generation and the specific NAGG design in achieving this success. To better understand the psychological impact of these goals, we conducted two studies using surveys of experience points and badges, commonly employed in gamified systems. Our findings reveal that, in the context of gamification, achievement goals influence users' motivation to engage, with higher levels of motivation evident among those with learning-oriented goals. Additionally, we discovered that, in comparison to gamification novices, experienced users exhibit decreased sensitivity to achievement goals and increased response to social influence. Furthermore, we found that, in the case of experienced users, the impact of achievement goals is largely mediated by their perceived level of personal relevance. Finally, we found that social influence has a more substantial effect on users' motivation when they are presented with achievement goals that are perceived as meaningful. These results contribute new insights to the field, potentially informing the design of more effective gamified systems. They also open up avenues for future research, including an in-depth examination of the interplay between social influence and personal relevance. Moreover, we suggest that, in the long term, repeated exposure to certain types of gamified systems may lead to a decline in users' sensitivity to achievement goals and a corresponding increase in their sensitivity to social influence. Lastly, we propose that future research investigate the potential for social influence to enhance motivation when users are presented with achievement goals that are perceived as relevant to their personal interests. The approach is similar to past derivations in utilizing conservation laws to determine an equation for an orbit. In this instance, trigonometry is employed to derive the comparison equation for an ellipse, without invoking calculus. The comparison involves calculating the radius of a circle at which a mass would have a gravitational force equal to that experienced at the orbiting radius, factoring in the orbiting object's velocity. The calculation yields a value approximately 3.35 times the orbiting radius, which corresponds to an eccentricity of about 0.25. The value of 3.37, obtained by summing the series for the orbiting velocity, is a more accurate representation. The comparison equation for an ellipse can be obtained by solving for the point on the orbit where the gravitational force and kinetic energy combine to result in a constant value, known as the total energy. The solution yields an equation that can be factored into two quadratic equations, one representing the semi-major axis and the other representing the distance from the focus. The equation for the orbit can be written as the difference between these two values, multiplied by the eccentricity, resulting in the elliptical shape. Alternatively, the equation for an orbit can be derived by applying conservation of angular momentum to determine the relationship between the radius and velocity, which, when combined with the equation for gravitational force, results in the equation for an ellipse. However, accurately modeling blood flow requires solving the Navier-Stokes equations for non-Newtonian, turbulent, and pulsatile flow under complex boundary conditions. Obtaining a detailed solution for these equations is computationally intensive, especially considering the need for spatial and temporal discretization and iterative solution convergence. To address this, a parallelizable algorithm based on the finite volume method was developed and implemented in an open-source computational framework. Aortic wall shear stress was also calculated and visualized, highlighting its spatial distribution and potential clinical implications. These findings confirm the ability of the computational framework to efficiently model complex aortic blood flow and inform further research and clinical applications. Additionally, the framework's modular architecture and parallelizable algorithm enable efficient simulation of a wide range of flow problems, facilitating future research in this field. Finally, the framework's open-source nature and user-friendly interface make it an accessible tool for a broad range of computational fluid dynamics applications. However, this technique is vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can manipulate the remote update aggregation process by bribing other users to submit fake updates.  To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that utilizes logical reasoning to detect counterfeit updates. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the potential vulnerabilities in the logical reasoning approach and highlights its value despite these weaknesses. we examine black holes with magnetic charges equivalent to those in Donaldson-Whitehead manifolds. To our surprise, these black holes possess regular horizons, implying they remain stable within the free energy framework. Additionally, their thermodynamic properties exhibit unique characteristics, particularly in regards to their scalar couplings, which diverge at the point of horizon formation and align with the charges' ratio in the free energy limit. Furthermore, we establish a connection between these black holes and a newly discovered superconformal field theory featuring a $SO(8)$ gauge group with a specific twist. This field theory is defined by a non-trivial three-form field with a specific relationship to the charges. We propose that the black holes' entropy is directly linked to the volume of a specific, non-compact Calabi-Yau manifold constructed using the black holes' magnetic charges. This proposal is supported by a separate study on the superconformal quantum mechanics model corresponding to the black holes. A 0.5mm diameter, 5mm long cylindrical sample was positioned between two copper blocks, with one block heated and the other cooled. Digital measurements of the sample's thermal resistance were taken every 0.1 seconds over the course of 100 seconds. A 2D heat-diffusion equation was used to simulate and analyze the results, which were then used to calculate the thermal conductivity of the graphite sample. The study found that the thermal conductivity of pyrolytic graphite at 300K is 0.70W/mK, with a margin of error of 0.04W/mK. As the temperature increased to 700K, the thermal conductivity also rose to 1.3W/mK. These results match previously reported values using different methods and indicate that the thermal conductivity of pyrolytic graphite has a linear relationship with temperature. The study also discovered that the thermal conductivity of the graphite sample was influenced by its crystallographic orientation and purity. The study's findings provide a basis for further research on the thermal conductivity of pyrolytic graphite and its potential applications in high-temperature technology. The study's method can also be applied to measure the thermal conductivity of other materials with complex structures. The study's data and calculations are available online for public access.

Our research indicates that to create massive stars, a cloud's magnetic field strength must be relatively low - less than 100 milligauss at a cloud density of 10,000 times the density of water. This finding contradicts earlier predictions, suggesting strongly magnetized clouds should rarely produce massive stars. This threshold is relatively stable, even when we change other factors such as the cloud's size and angular momentum. The clouds that produce massive stars in our simulations are typically the oldest and most isolated, which may explain why massive stars are less common in the centers of galaxies and more common in less crowded areas. The Cable System Control Problem involves finding a signal that, when transmitted through the cable, results in the cable's end point coinciding with a desired signal at the cable's terminus at a specified time. The control problem is further refined to optimize the required signal, known as the control current, under an $L^2$-norm constraint. This approximation method relies on the solution of a nonlinear equation resulting from the application of the implicit function theorem. Notably, our proposed method enables the computation of optimal controls that are discontinuous, a feat that was previously unachievable using existing methods. We validate the efficacy of our approach by successfully calculating the optimal control for a non-trivial cable system. However, these expansions fail when applied to brief, intense processes, which require a new method of expansion, described in this paper. This new method, which will be referred to as the Chapman--Enskog--Neumann (CEN) approach, can be applied to any kinetic model. By contrast to conventional Chapman--Enskog expansions, which result in fluid equations that disagree with energy conservation, the CEN approach yields a generalized hydrodynamic system that adheres to energy conservation as well as second-order fluid dynamics. Furthermore, the CEN approach can be applied to scenarios involving small numbers of particles, which are characterized by low densities and short timescales. This phenomenon, which arises from interactions between light and a relativistic electron, cannot be modeled using conventional kinetic methods

To this end, we examine multiple text representation methods in a controlled experiment and find that BERT and word embeddings excel in a supervised hate speech classification task but underperform in a semi-supervised text segmentation task within the same domain.
Conversely, we discover that a convolutional neural network leveraging filters from pre-trained UNK- and OOV-sensitive word embeddings outperforms other representations in a text segmentation task, underscoring the significance of word embeddings in hate speech classification. 
To address concerns about the interpretation of sensitive features, we suggest two approaches: removing sensitive features from training and using a differential privacy tool. 
Ultimately, our research reveals that the choice of text representation heavily influences performance in hate speech classification and segmentation tasks. 
Given this, we propose that future projects should carefully select a text representation method tailored to their specific requirements. 
The findings of this study are further validated through the application of our models to additional, diverse hate speech datasets. 
The source code and dataset used in this research are publicly available for reproduction and further development. 
Additionally, we introduce a new, challenging task in classifying hate speech within nested comments on social media platforms.

Since digital-analog duality involves a continuous process, it can be observed only under the influence of noise, which is present in all real quantum computers. Traditionally, this task relies on a straightforward approach involving two stages: first, a passage is selected, and then phrases from it are compared to those in the question. Existing methods focus on the second stage, treating the first as a given. Surprisingly, little research has been done to evaluate passage selection techniques. As a result, the initial stage of this process is often overlooked. Different theoretical models yield significantly different results, with some indicating a steep decline in mass among the most massive stars and others suggesting a relatively flat line.  In an effort to resolve this discrepancy, we conducted a series of high-resolution, three-dimensional numerical simulations to examine the behavior of H II regions surrounding massive stars with masses ranging from 120 to 250,000 solar masses.  These simulations took into account the complex processes of radiative pressure, gas absorption, and dust emission that influence the gas ionization and excitation patterns. Additionally, we discovered that the observed R23 and Petti parameters are highly sensitive to the mass of the most massive stars and the ionization factor of the hydrogen. which are a prevalent type of blockchain-based trading platforms. 
We find that the order process has two distinct phases: one in which the strategy 
appears unpredictable to traders, resulting in a market equilibrium that benefits the operator, 
and another where the operator's advantage is diminished due to a loss in perceived randomness. 
To achieve the first phase, the AMM must maintain a strategy that is distinct from its history. 
We also identify specific conditions under which the operator's advantage is based on randomness, 
not just the order process itself. 
As a result, the operator's gain can be eliminated if traders use a model that accurately predicts the probability distribution 
of future orders, rather than simply relying on past behavior. 
We further demonstrate the validity of our analysis through real-world market observations.

The learning trajectory in deep neural networks often exhibits a peculiar pattern, where early stages typically concentrate on simpler tasks and later stages frequently involve more complex tasks. As a replacement for the OpenMP parallelization approach, this thread pool leverages Python to enhance the flexibility and portability of its applications. By effectively distributing workloads to local CPU cores, even-handed execution is achieved, thereby amplifying the overall computational speed. A detailed examination of its underlying architecture, along with a description of the associated implementation strategies, is provided below.

## Key Components

### 1. Work Item Management

A work item is an instance of a function along with its necessary arguments. To manage these items, a custom queue was developed, which supports thread-safe addition and removal of work items. This queue facilitates the efficient distribution of work items to local CPU cores.

### 2. Thread Creation

To create threads, the `threading` module from Python's standard library is utilized. However, due to Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), which limits concurrent execution to a single thread, the overall benefit of multi-threading is maximized when combined with CPU-bound tasks.

### 3. Thread Pool

A custom thread pool class was designed to manage a pool of pre-created threads. This pool dynamically adjusts the number of threads based on the available CPU cores and the specified maximum pool size. To submit tasks to the pool, the `submit` method is provided, which adds the task to the queue and assigns it to an available thread.

The measurement problem in quantum theory poses a significant challenge, with various solutions proposed over the years. One such proposal, the pilot-wave interpretation developed by Eugene Wigner, John Archibald Wheeler, and Albert Einstein, offers insights into the nature of reality. This interpretation, akin to the macrorealism underlying classical physics, treats the wavefunction as a tool to track a physical reality defined by a well-defined configuration. It assigns real values to probabilities, resolving the measurement problem by eliminating any ambiguity. 

Applying this interpretation to the theory of superconductivity yields two key results. Firstly, it demonstrates that Cooper pairs emerge as a physical phenomenon, resulting from the interaction between electrons and phonons, which are themselves physical entities. Secondly, it shows that the wavefunction, or more accurately, the configuration, represents the macroscopic physical state of superconducting materials. This state, governed by the Schrödinger equation, determines the macroscopic quantum properties of superconductors.

MacPherson developed a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the details of their method and explore its underlying principles. We also use this approach to derive a simplified combinatorial formula for the first Pontrjagin class of a manifold with a square-root connection. A square-root connection is a connection on the cotangent bundle of a manifold, characterized by a self-adjoint property with respect to a globally defined inner product. We find that the first Pontrjagin class of such a connection is directly represented by the Stiefel-Whitney class $w_2$ of the underlying vector bundle. We provide two distinct proofs of this result. Firstly, we utilize a spectral sequence, relating the homology of a configuration space to the cohomology of a manifold with a square-root connection. Secondly, we apply a homotopy-theoretic approach, involving the homotopy quotient of a square-root connection. We demonstrate that these two approaches yield the same expression for the first Pontrjagin class. We also discuss the generalization of this result to higher Pontrjagin classes. Additionally, we explore the application of this result to a specific manifold, derived from the group $SO_3$. We calculate its Pontrjagin classes explicitly. We also investigate the limit behavior of these classes as the rank of the group increases to $SO_n$.

The dataset includes detailed annotations for individual fingers, comprising precise 2D and 3D joint localizations, facilitating a wide range of applications across computer vision and robotics. The HUMBI dataset is publicly accessible at https://github.com/aim-hub-hands/hands_dataset.\\

Starting from a simplified model of weakly interacting layers, we show how the long-range dispersion forces between layers, as described by the Hamaker constant, contribute to a decrease in interlayer energy in proportion to the inverse sixth power of separation distance. This leads to a significant impact on interlayer stability, particularly noticeable when layers comprise materials with significantly varying dielectric properties. We then investigate the role of short-range interactions within each layer, using a case study of MoS$_2$. Our analysis with the first-principles calculations shows that taking long-range van der Waals interactions into account correctly predicts a highly stable layered structure, in contrast to predictions made without considering these interactions. Our research provides foundational insights into the design of van der Waals heterostructures with tunable interlayer distances.
